verse.text: The beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ.

note.traditional: Jesus Christ, the Son of God

verse.note: Most manuscripts, and most English translations, continue with “the Son of God.” The words are absent from some early witnesses, and the Greek edition translated here omits them. Scholars are divided on whether a copyist dropped them by accident or added them as a natural expansion of the title.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for the public announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler’s accession. “Gospel” has become a religious term and a book title, which hides that sense. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: Just as it is written in Isaiah the prophet, “Look, I am sending my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way;
verse.note: The quotation is a composite. The words in verse 2 echo Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1, and only verse 3 comes from Isaiah (40:3). Later manuscripts read “in the prophets,” probably to resolve the difficulty.

text.q: a voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight,’”

verse.text: so John the Baptizer appeared in the wilderness, proclaiming a baptism of turning back for the forgiveness of sins.
verse.note: “Repentance” now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repentance” and “repent” as established terms that readers understand to include a change of life.

verse.text: The whole Judean countryside and all the people of Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.
John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey.
And he proclaimed, “The one who is stronger than I am is coming after me; I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the strap of his sandals.

text.q: I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

verse.text: In those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized in the Jordan by John.
And immediately, as he was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit coming down on him like a dove.
verse.note: The Greek is plural in both this verse and the next, a Semitic turn of phrase for God’s dwelling. Most translations flatten the plural to “heaven,” at least in verse 11. It is kept here in both places.

verse.text: And a voice came from the heavens: “You are my Son, the beloved; with you I am well pleased.”
And immediately the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.
He was in the wilderness forty days, being tested by Satan. He was with the wild animals, and the angels were serving him.
verse.note: The verb means to put to the test. In the Greek Old Testament it is the usual word for God testing Israel in the wilderness, a background the forty days recall. Most translations use “tempted” here, and the lexicons recognize both senses; which fits this scene better is disputed.

verse.text: After John was handed over, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the good news of God
verse.note: Most translations say John was “arrested” or “put in prison,” which is what happened. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s power. Mark later uses the same verb for what is done to Jesus and what will be done to his followers, and this rendering lets that link show.

verse.text: and saying, “The time has been fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near. Turn back and believe in the good news.”
verse.note: The Greek perfect can mean that the kingdom has drawn close and is about to arrive, or that it has in effect arrived. “Has come near” leaves the same openness as the Greek. Scholars remain divided on which nuance Mark intends.

verse.text: As he was passing along beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, Simon’s brother, casting nets in the sea, for they were fishermen.
Jesus said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of people.”
And immediately they left their nets and followed him.
Going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother; they too were in a boat, mending the nets,
and immediately he called them. They left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and went off after him.
They went into Capernaum, and immediately, on the Sabbath, he began teaching in the synagogue.
They were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.
And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out,

text.q: “What do you have to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!”

verse.text: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!”
The unclean spirit convulsed him, cried out with a loud voice, and came out of him.
They were all amazed, so that they began asking one another, “What is this? A new teaching! With authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.”
And the report about him immediately went out everywhere, into the whole surrounding region of Galilee.
And immediately, on leaving the synagogue, they went into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.
Simon’s mother-in-law was lying down with a fever, and immediately they told him about her.
He went to her, took her by the hand, and raised her up. The fever left her, and she began to serve them.
When evening came, after the sun had set, people were bringing to him all who were sick and those possessed by demons.
The whole town was gathered at the door.
He healed many who were sick with various diseases and drove out many demons, and he would not let the demons speak, because they knew him.
Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he got up, went out, and went away to a deserted place, and there he was praying.
Simon and those with him hunted for him,
and they found him and said to him, “Everyone is looking for you.”
He said to them, “Let us go elsewhere, to the neighboring market towns, so that I may proclaim there too, for that is why I came out.”
And he went throughout all Galilee, proclaiming in their synagogues and driving out the demons.
A man with a skin disease came to him, pleading with him and kneeling, and said to him, “If you are willing, you can make me clean.”
verse.note: The Greek term covers the range of scaly skin conditions regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which made a person ritually unclean; this is why the man asks to be made “clean.” “Leper” today means Hansen’s disease, which is narrower and may not even be included. Most translations keep “leper,” usually with a footnote, partly because “skin disease” can understate the social exclusion involved.

verse.text: Angered, Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said to him, “I am willing. Be made clean.”
verse.note: Nearly all manuscripts read “moved with compassion,” and most translations follow them. A few witnesses read “angered,” and the Greek edition translated here adopts that reading as the one scribes were more likely to soften. If it is original, the object of the anger is not stated; suggestions include the disease and its effects on the man.

verse.text: Immediately the skin disease left him, and he was made clean.
With a stern warning Jesus immediately sent him away,
verse.note: The Greek verb expresses strong emotion, often indignation, and elsewhere describes a harsh rebuke. Here it may mean a forceful warning, as translated, or a display of agitation. The verb rendered “sent him away” is also strong; it is the one used in this chapter for driving out demons.

verse.text: saying to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”
verse.note: The phrase may mean proof to the priests, or to people generally, that the man is clean and that the Law has been observed. It can also be read as “a testimony against them,” that is, evidence that will count against those who do not respond. The Greek allows either.

verse.text: But the man went out and began to proclaim it widely and to spread the story, so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly but stayed outside in deserted places; and people kept coming to him from everywhere.
When he came back into Capernaum some days later, word got out that he was at home.
So many gathered that there was no longer any room, not even around the door, and he was speaking the word to them.
Some people came, bringing to him a paralyzed man carried by four of them.
Since they could not bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above where he was, and when they had dug through, they lowered the mat on which the paralyzed man was lying.
verse.note: The Greek word names a poor person’s pallet or light stretcher, something one person could roll up and carry. “Bed,” the rendering of the older versions, suggests furniture to a modern reader; most recent translations also use “mat.”

Ordinary Galilean houses had flat roofs of wooden beams covered with branches or reeds and packed clay, reached by an outside stairway or ladder. Opening such a roof meant literally digging through it.

verse.text: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralyzed man, “Child, your sins are forgiven.”
verse.note: The Greek word means “child” without specifying gender and was used as an affectionate address by an elder or teacher. Most English versions render it “Son” here; the word for “son” in the phrase “Son of Man” (verse 10) is a different one.

verse.text: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, reasoning in their hearts,

text.q: “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

verse.note: Literally “except one, God.” The wording may simply mean “God alone,” or it may deliberately echo Israel’s confession that God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4); the Greek allows either.

verse.text: Immediately Jesus, aware in his spirit that they were reasoning this way within themselves, said to them, “Why are you reasoning about these things in your hearts?

text.q: Which is easier: to say to the paralyzed man, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?

verse.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” he said to the paralyzed man,
verse.note: This is Jesus’s characteristic way of referring to himself in the Gospels. Behind it lies a Semitic idiom meaning “a human being,” and many scholars also hear an allusion to the figure “like a son of man” who is given authority in Daniel 7:13–14. How much of each sense is intended in a given saying is debated.

text.q: “I say to you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”

verse.text: He got up, immediately picked up his mat, and went out in front of everyone, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”
He went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd kept coming to him, and he taught them.
As he was passing by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
verse.note: Capernaum lay near the border of Herod Antipas’s territory, and Levi was probably collecting tolls or customs duties on goods in transit rather than direct taxes. Such collectors were widely regarded as dishonest and as compromised by their work, which is why they are paired with “sinners” in the next verses.

verse.text: And as he was reclining at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many of them, and they were following him.
verse.note: The Greek does not say whose house this is. Most interpreters take it to be Levi’s, as Luke 5:29 states outright, but Mark’s wording could also mean Jesus’s own home in Capernaum. Guests at a formal meal reclined on couches or cushions rather than sitting.

verse.text: When the scribes of the Pharisees saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, they said to his disciples, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “the scribes and the Pharisees,” a more familiar phrase, and the older English versions follow them. The earlier and harder reading, adopted here, refers to scribes who belonged to the Pharisaic party.

verse.text: On hearing this, Jesus said to them, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?”
Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.
verse.note: Literally “the sons of the bridal chamber,” a Semitic idiom for the bridegroom’s friends and attendants or, more broadly, the guests at the wedding. A wedding celebration could last a week, and fasting during it would have been unthinkable.

text.q: But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast, on that day.
No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. Otherwise the patch pulls away from it, the new from the old, and the tear becomes worse.
And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the wine will burst the skins, and the wine is lost, and the skins too. Rather, new wine into fresh wineskins.”

verse.text: One Sabbath he was passing through the grainfields, and his disciples began to make their way, plucking the heads of grain.
verse.note: The Greek phrase normally means “to make a road,” and a few interpreters think the disciples were clearing a path through the grain. Most take it as equivalent to “make their way,” with the plucking as the point at issue; Deuteronomy 23:25 allowed plucking a neighbor’s grain by hand, so the objection concerns doing it on the Sabbath.

verse.text: The Pharisees said to him, “Look, why are they doing what is not permitted on the Sabbath?”
And he said to them, “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and hungry, he and those with him—

text.q: how he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not permitted for anyone but the priests to eat, and gave some also to those who were with him?”

note.term: in the time of Abiathar the high priest

verse.note: In the account in 1 Samuel 21:1–6 the priest who gives David the bread is Ahimelech; Abiathar was his son and became the well-known high priest of David’s reign. The Greek phrase may mean loosely “in the days of Abiathar,” or possibly “in the passage about Abiathar,” and the difficulty is long recognized; Matthew and Luke do not include the phrase.

verse.text: And he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for people, and not people for the Sabbath.
verse.note: The traditional “The Sabbath was made for man” uses “man” for humanity in general. The Greek word is the same one found in “Son of Man” in the next verse, so the two sayings are linked. Most interpreters take “Son of Man” there as Jesus’s self-designation, though some think the saying originally meant that human beings have authority over the Sabbath.

text.q: So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

verse.text: Again he went into a synagogue, and a man was there who had a withered hand.
They were watching him closely to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.
He said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand in the middle.”
Then he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill?” But they were silent.
Looking around at them with anger, deeply grieved at the hardness of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
The Pharisees went out and at once began plotting with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.
verse.note: Supporters of the Herodian dynasty, here probably partisans of Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee. They are mentioned only in Mark and Matthew, and little else is known about them. The Pharisees were not natural allies of Herod’s house, so the alliance shows how serious the opposition had become.

verse.text: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great multitude from Galilee followed. And from Judea
and from Jerusalem and from Idumea and beyond the Jordan and around Tyre and Sidon, a great multitude, hearing all that he was doing, came to him.
He told his disciples to keep a small boat ready for him because of the crowd, so that they would not crush him;
for he had healed many, so that all who had afflictions were pressing in on him to touch him.
And the unclean spirits, whenever they saw him, would fall down before him and cry out, “You are the Son of God!”
And he sternly warned them not to make him known.
Then he went up the mountain and called to him those whom he himself wanted, and they came to him.
He appointed twelve, so that they might be with him and so that he might send them out to proclaim
verse.note: Many early manuscripts add “whom he also named apostles” after “twelve,” and some editions print those words in brackets; they may have been copied in from Luke 6:13. The SBLGNT omits them, and this translation follows it. The repeated “He appointed the Twelve” in verse 16 is likewise missing from many manuscripts.

verse.text: and to have authority to drive out the demons.
He appointed the Twelve: Simon, to whom he gave the name Peter;
James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to them he gave the name Boanerges, which means Sons of Thunder);
verse.note: Mark transliterates a Semitic nickname and then translates it for his Greek-speaking readers. The first part reflects the word for “sons of,” but the exact Hebrew or Aramaic behind the second part is uncertain.

verse.text: Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Cananaean,

note.traditional: Simon the Canaanite (KJV); Simon the Zealot (NIV, ESV)

verse.note: The byname has nothing to do with Canaan or Cana. It transliterates an Aramaic word meaning “zealous one,” which Luke 6:15 translates as “the Zealot.” Mark leaves it untranslated, and it is kept here as a name. Whether it points to personal zeal for the Law or to links with a militant movement is debated.

verse.text: and Judas Iscariot, who also handed him over.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing a person into someone else’s custody. The Gospels use the same word for what the priests and Pilate later do to Jesus. Most English versions say “betrayed” when Judas is the subject, and some scholars defend that as a legitimate contextual sense. “Handed over” lets the reader see the chain of handings-over that the Greek reader saw.

verse.text: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat a meal.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “he comes into a house.” Without the article the phrase can mean “home,” probably the house in Capernaum mentioned in 2:1, or simply “into a house.”

verse.text: When his family heard of it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.”

note.traditional: his friends (KJV); his family (NRSV, ESV, NIV)

verse.note: The Greek is literally “those from beside him,” an idiom that in this period usually meant a person’s relatives or household. Verse 31 suggests his mother and brothers are meant, though some take the phrase more broadly as his associates. “They were saying” can also be read impersonally, “people were saying,” in which case the family acts on a report and does not itself pass the judgment.

verse.text: And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, “He has Beelzebul,” and, “By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.”
verse.note: A name for the ruler of the demons, whom Jesus’ reply identifies with Satan. It probably goes back to a title of an old Canaanite deity (compare Baal-zebub in 2 Kings 1), though its exact meaning is disputed. The KJV’s “Beelzebub” follows the Latin tradition, not the Greek manuscripts.

verse.text: So he called them to him and spoke to them in parables: “How can Satan drive out Satan?

text.q: If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.
And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.
And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand; his end has come.
But no one can enter the strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first ties up the strong man; then he will plunder his house.
Truly I tell you, everything will be forgiven the sons of men—their sins and whatever blasphemies they utter;

verse.note: A Semitic idiom for human beings in general, kept because the Greek preserves it. It is the plural of the phrase behind “Son of Man,” but here it is not a title.

text.q: but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness but is guilty of an eternal sin.”

verse.note: Later manuscripts read “eternal judgment,” which lies behind the KJV’s “eternal damnation”; the earliest witnesses read “sin.” In Greek, “never” is literally “not into the age,” and “eternal” is the adjective formed from the same word, so the two halves of the verse echo each other.

verse.text: He said this because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”
Then his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside, they sent word to him, calling him.
A crowd was sitting around him, and they told him, “Look, your mother and your brothers are outside, looking for you.”
verse.note: Some manuscripts add “and your sisters,” and some editions print those words in brackets. The SBLGNT omits them. They may have been added in view of “sister” in verse 35, or dropped to match verses 31, 33 and 34.

verse.text: He answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?”
And looking around at those seated in a circle around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers!

text.q: For whoever does the will of God, that one is my brother and sister and mother.”

verse.text: Again he began to teach beside the sea. A very large crowd gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, while the whole crowd was on the land, facing the sea.
verse.note: Mark calls the freshwater Lake of Galilee a “sea,” following Semitic usage in which one word covers any large body of water. The rendering keeps “sea” because the storm scene that closes the chapter draws on Old Testament language about God mastering the sea.

verse.text: He taught them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word translates a Hebrew term covering proverbs, riddles, taunts and extended comparisons. A first-century hearer would not have limited it to illustrative stories. The wider sense, including “riddle,” matters for verse 11, where everything comes “in parables” to outsiders.

text.q: “Listen! Look, a sower went out to sow.
And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and ate it up.
Other seed fell on the rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and it sprang up at once because it had no depth of soil.
And when the sun rose it was scorched, and because it had no root it withered.
Other seed fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked it, and it yielded no crop.
And other seeds fell into the good soil and yielded a crop, coming up and growing, and bore thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.”

verse.text: And he said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let them hear.”
When he was alone, those around him, together with the Twelve, asked him about the parables.
He said to them, “To you the secret of the kingdom of God has been given, but to those outside everything comes in parables,
verse.note: In Jewish Greek of the period, notably the Greek book of Daniel, this word is the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, which is not the point. Many versions keep “mystery” as an established term, though several (RSV, NRSV, NIV) also use “secret” in this saying.

text.q: so that they may look and look yet not see, and hear and hear yet not understand; otherwise they might turn back and be forgiven.”

verse.note: The words echo Isaiah 6:9–10, in a form closer to the Aramaic synagogue paraphrase (“be forgiven”) than to the Hebrew or the Greek version (“be healed”). The conjunction normally expresses purpose, and many scholars read it so here: the parables carry out the judgment Isaiah announced on unresponsive hearers. Others take it as result (“with the result that”) or as shorthand for “so that Scripture is fulfilled,” and some read the last clause as “unless perhaps they turn.” The rendering keeps the plain purpose sense and does not resolve the difficulty.

verse.text: And he said to them, “You do not understand this parable? Then how will you understand all the parables?

text.q: The sower sows the word.
These are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear it, Satan comes at once and takes away the word that was sown in them.
And these, likewise, are the ones sown on the rocky ground: when they hear the word, they at once receive it with joy,
yet they have no root in themselves and last only for a time; then, when affliction or persecution comes because of the word, at once they fall away.

verse.note: The verb comes from the Greek Old Testament’s word for a trap or obstacle and means to be tripped up in one’s loyalty to God. The King James Version’s “are offended” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak for people who abandon the word under persecution. Most modern versions also have “fall away” here.

text.q: Others are the ones sown among the thorns: these are the ones who have heard the word,
but the worries of the age, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desires for everything else come in and choke the word, and it yields no crop.

verse.note: The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, here the present age as contrasted with the age to come. “World” blurs this and suggests a different Greek word. Lexicons accept “age” here, though many versions keep “world.”

text.q: And those are the ones sown on the good soil: they hear the word and welcome it and yield a crop, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “Does the lamp come to be put under the basket or under the bed? Does it not come to be put on the lampstand?
verse.note: The Greek says literally that the lamp “comes,” with the definite article, and most versions smooth this to “is a lamp brought.” It may be no more than a loose idiom. Many interpreters, however, think the odd wording hints at the coming of Jesus or of the kingdom, hidden now but meant to be revealed, so the literal verb is kept.
The word names a household vessel for measuring grain, holding roughly two gallons (about nine liters). “Bushel,” the traditional rendering, is a much larger measure and now an unfamiliar one.

text.q: For nothing is hidden except to be disclosed, nor has anything been concealed except to come into the open.
If anyone has ears to hear, let them hear.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you measure with, it will be measured to you, and more will be added to you.

text.q: For to the one who has, it will be given; and from the one who does not have, even what that person has will be taken away.”

verse.text: And he said, “The kingdom of God is like this: it is as if someone scatters seed on the earth

text.q: and sleeps and rises, night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he himself does not know how.
On its own the earth yields a crop: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.
But when the crop is ripe, at once he sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

verse.note: The verb normally means “hand over.” Here alone in the New Testament it is used of a crop, with no object. Most scholars take it to mean “permits,” that is, the crop is ready for harvest, and nearly all modern versions have “is ripe”; a few suggest “yields itself.”

note.term: he sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come

verse.note: The wording echoes Joel 3:13, where sending in the sickle at harvest is a picture of God’s final judgment. A hearer who knew the prophets would have caught the reference, which gives the quiet growth of the seed a decisive end.

verse.text: And he said, “To what shall we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it?

text.q: It is like a mustard seed, which, when it is sown on the earth, is smaller than all the seeds on the earth,
yet when it is sown, it comes up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the sky can nest in its shade.”

note.term: the birds of the sky can nest in its shade

verse.note: The picture recalls the great tree of Ezekiel 17:23 and 31:6 and Daniel 4:12, in whose branches or shade the birds lodge. That tree is an image of a kingdom sheltering many peoples. Applying it to a garden shrub grown from a tiny seed is part of the parable’s point.

verse.text: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as far as they were able to hear it.
He did not speak to them without a parable, but in private he explained everything to his own disciples.
On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us cross over to the other side.”
Leaving the crowd, they took him along in the boat, just as he was; and other boats were with him.
A great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling.
But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”
He woke up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Quiet! Be silent!” And the wind died down, and there was a great calm.
verse.note: The second command uses a verb meaning literally “muzzle” and commonly “silence.” Jesus uses the same verb to silence an unclean spirit at Mark 1:25, and the narrator’s word “rebuked” appears in both scenes. The traditional “Peace! Be still!” is gentler than the Greek, which addresses the sea as a hostile power being shut up.

verse.text: He said to them, “Why are you cowardly? Do you still have no faith?”
verse.note: The Greek adjective means timid or cowardly and is a reproach. It is a different word from the “fear” of the next verse, which is closer to awe. Most versions use “afraid” or “fearful” for both, which hides the contrast between the cowardice Jesus rebukes and the great fear that follows the calm.

verse.text: And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
They came to the other side of the sea, to the region of the Gerasenes.
verse.note: Manuscripts differ here between “Gerasenes,” “Gadarenes,” and “Gergesenes.” Gerasa lay roughly thirty miles southeast of the lake, which is probably why copyists substituted the names of nearer places. Most editors judge “Gerasenes” to be the original reading in Mark.

verse.text: When he got out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet him.
He lived among the tombs, and no one could bind him any longer, not even with a chain,
because he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he had torn the chains apart and smashed the shackles, and no one was strong enough to subdue him.
Constantly, night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he was crying out and cutting himself with stones.
When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and bowed down before him,
verse.note: The Greek verb names the act of prostrating oneself, and what it signifies depends on who does it and to whom. Here a possessed man throws himself down before a superior power he fears, so the gesture is rendered instead of “worship,” which in modern English implies devotion. Most recent versions likewise have “bowed down” or “fell on his knees” here.

verse.text: and crying out in a loud voice he said, “What do you have to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I charge you by God, do not torment me!”
verse.note: The verb means to put someone under a solemn oath, and it was the kind of formula exorcists used to command spirits (compare Acts 19:13). Here the roles are reversed: the spirit tries the exorcist’s formula on Jesus, and it has no effect.

verse.text: For he had been saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!”
And he asked him, “What is your name?” He said to him, “My name is Legion, for we are many.”
verse.note: A Latin military term for the main unit of the Roman army, some five to six thousand soldiers at full strength. As the speaker explains, it stands here for a very large number. Whether Mark also intends an allusion to the Roman occupation is debated.

verse.text: And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the region.
Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside,
and they begged him, “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.”
He gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand of them, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and were drowned in the sea.
Those who had been tending them fled and reported it in the town and in the countryside, and people came to see what it was that had happened.
They came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind—the very man who had had the legion—and they were afraid.
Those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man, and told them about the pigs.
And they began to beg him to leave their territory.
As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged him that he might be with him.
He did not let him, but said to him, “Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he had mercy on you.”
verse.note: Spoken by Jesus, “the Lord” most naturally refers to God, and Luke’s parallel has “God.” The next verse, however, has the man proclaim what “Jesus” had done for him, and Mark may intend the reader to notice the overlap.

verse.text: So he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone was amazed.
verse.note: A group of ten Hellenistic cities, most of them east of the Jordan, with largely non-Jewish populations. The herd of pigs, animals unclean under the Law, has already signaled that the scene is set in Gentile territory.

verse.text: When Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea.
One of the synagogue leaders, named Jairus, came, and when he saw him he fell at his feet
and begged him earnestly, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.”
So he went with him. A large crowd was following him and pressing in on him.
Now there was a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.
verse.note: The phrase echoes the Greek of Leviticus 15, where chronic bleeding of this kind makes a woman ritually unclean, along with whatever she touches. Mark does not mention impurity, and scholars disagree about how far it shapes the scene. It may help explain her secrecy and her fear.

verse.text: She had endured much under many doctors and had spent everything she had, yet she had gained nothing by it but had instead grown worse.
She had heard about Jesus, and she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak,
for she was saying, “If I touch even his clothes, I will be made well.”
Immediately the source of her bleeding dried up, and she knew in her body that she was healed of her affliction.
And immediately Jesus, aware in himself that power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and said, “Who touched my clothes?”
His disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing in on you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”
But he kept looking around to see the woman who had done this.
Then the woman, afraid and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your affliction.”
verse.note: The verb here and in verses 23 and 28 is the one usually translated “save.” In Greek it covers rescue from any danger, including illness, and in this story physical healing is the primary sense. Many interpreters think Mark also means the reader to hear the wider sense, “your faith has saved you.”

verse.text: While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house and said, “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?”
But Jesus, ignoring what was said, told the synagogue leader, “Do not be afraid; only believe.”
verse.note: The Greek verb can mean either “overhear” or “pay no attention to, disregard.” The second is its regular sense in the Septuagint and at Matthew 18:17, and is followed here, but many translations have “overhearing” and either fits the scene. Many later manuscripts read simply “hearing,” which is the reading behind the King James Version.

verse.text: He did not let anyone accompany him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James.
They came to the synagogue leader’s house, and he saw a commotion, with people weeping and wailing loudly.
He went in and said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child has not died but is sleeping.”
And they laughed at him. But he put them all out, took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him, and went in where the child was.
Taking the child by the hand, he said to her, “Talitha koum,” which translated means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!”
verse.note: These words are Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus and of Galilee, which Mark preserves and then translates for his Greek-speaking readers. Many manuscripts read “koumi,” the grammatically feminine form of the imperative. The phrase “I say to you” in Mark’s translation is not represented in the Aramaic words themselves.

verse.text: Immediately the girl got up and began walking around, for she was twelve years old. And immediately they were overcome with great astonishment.
He gave them strict orders that no one should know about this, and told them to give her something to eat.
He went out from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him.

When the Sabbath came, he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, “Where did this man get these things? What is this wisdom that has been given to him, and such deeds of power done through his hands?
verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used here of concrete acts that display it. “Deeds of power” keeps visible the link with verse 14, where the same word describes the “powers” at work in Jesus. There is no dispute about the meaning, and “miracles,” used by many translations, is an equally acceptable rendering.

verse.text: Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And aren’t his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a craftsman who builds or makes things, most often in wood, though it could also cover work in stone. “Carpenter” is the traditional rendering and remains the likeliest, but some scholars prefer the broader “builder” or “craftsman.”

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household.”
And he could not do any deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them.
And he was amazed at their unbelief. Then he went around the surrounding villages, teaching.
He called the Twelve to him and began to send them out two by two, and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
He instructed them to take nothing for the journey except a staff alone: no bread, no bag, no money in their belts,
but to wear sandals, and not to put on two tunics.
And he said to them, “Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave that place.

text.q: And if any place does not welcome you and they will not listen to you, as you leave there shake off the dust under your feet as a testimony against them.”

verse.text: So they went out and proclaimed that people should turn back,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repent,” which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Turn back” is used for that reason.

verse.text: and they drove out many demons, and anointed many sick people with oil and healed them.
King Herod heard of it, for the name of Jesus had become well known, and people were saying, “John the Baptizer has been raised from the dead, and that is why the powers are at work in him.”
verse.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome. His official title was tetrarch, as Matthew and Luke call him. Mark’s “king” probably reflects popular usage.

Many manuscripts read “he was saying,” which makes Herod the speaker; this is the reading behind the King James Version. The text translated here has the plural, which fits the list of popular opinions continued in verse 15. Herod’s own verdict then comes in verse 16.

verse.text: But others were saying, “He is Elijah,” and others were saying, “A prophet, like one of the prophets.”
But when Herod heard, he said, “John, the man I beheaded—he has been raised!”
For it was Herod himself who had sent and had John arrested and bound in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, because he had married her.
For John had been telling Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
So Herodias held a grudge against him and wanted to kill him, but she could not,
for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he listened to him he was greatly perplexed, and yet he liked to listen to him.
verse.note: The majority of later manuscripts read “he did many things,” a difference of a few letters in Greek. Several early and important manuscripts read “he was greatly perplexed,” which most modern editions and translations follow.

verse.text: Then an opportune day came, when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles, his commanders, and the leading men of Galilee.
Herodias’s own daughter came in and danced, and she pleased Herod and his dinner guests. The king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you want, and I will give it to you.”
verse.note: Some early manuscripts read “his daughter Herodias,” which would make the girl Herod’s daughter and give her the same name as her mother. The text translated here reads “the daughter of Herodias herself,” in agreement with Matthew 14:6. The Jewish historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter by her first marriage as Salome; Mark does not name her.

verse.text: And he swore to her, “Whatever you ask me for, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.”
She went out and said to her mother, “What should I ask for?” She said, “The head of John the Baptizer.”
At once she hurried back in to the king and made her request: “I want you to give me, right now, the head of John the Baptist on a platter.”
The king was deeply distressed, but because of his oaths and his dinner guests he did not want to refuse her.
So at once the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. The man went and beheaded him in the prison,
brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.
When his disciples heard of it, they came and took away his body and laid it in a tomb.
The apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him everything they had done and taught.
He said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they did not even have a chance to eat.
So they went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.
But many saw them leaving and recognized them, and they ran there together on foot from all the towns and arrived ahead of them.
When he got out of the boat, he saw a large crowd, and he was moved with compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.
When it was already late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a deserted place, and it is already late.

text.q: Send them away so that they can go to the surrounding farms and villages and buy themselves something to eat.”

verse.text: But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” They said to him, “Are we to go and spend two hundred denarii on bread and give it to them to eat?”
verse.note: The denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s wage for a laborer (compare Matthew 20:2). The sum the disciples mention is therefore more than half a year’s pay.

verse.text: He said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” When they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.”
Then he ordered them to have everyone recline, group by group, on the green grass.
They reclined row by row, by hundreds and by fifties.
verse.note: The Greek repeats a word meaning “garden beds,” picturing the crowd laid out in neat plots on the grass. The matching phrase in verse 39, “group by group,” repeats a word for dinner parties. The doubled words are a Semitic way of saying “in group after group,” and the repetition is kept in English.

verse.text: Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, said the blessing, broke the loaves, and kept giving them to his disciples to set before the people; and he divided the two fish among them all.
They all ate and were satisfied,
and they picked up twelve baskets full of broken pieces, and of the fish as well.
Those who had eaten the loaves were five thousand men.
At once he made his disciples get into the boat and go on ahead to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he himself sent the crowd away.
After taking leave of them, he went off to the mountain to pray.
When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and he was alone on the land.
He saw them straining at the oars, for the wind was against them. About the fourth watch of the night he came toward them, walking on the sea, and he meant to pass by them.

note.term: the fourth watch of the night

verse.note: The Roman reckoning divided the night into four watches. The fourth was the last, roughly three to six in the morning, so the disciples had been rowing for most of the night.

The words can mean simply that Jesus intended to walk past the boat. Many scholars hear instead an echo of Old Testament scenes in which God “passes by” to reveal himself (Exodus 33:19–22; 1 Kings 19:11), and of Job 9:8–11, where God walks on the sea and passes by. The rendering leaves both readings open.

verse.text: But when they saw him walking on the sea, they thought it was a ghost and cried out,
for they all saw him and were terrified. But at once he spoke with them and said, “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally “I am,” the ordinary way of saying “It’s me.” The same words are also God’s self-declaration in the Greek Old Testament (for example Isaiah 43:10), and in a scene of walking on the sea many interpreters think Mark intends that echo. Whether he does is disputed; the everyday sense is certain.

verse.text: Then he climbed into the boat with them, and the wind died down. They were utterly astounded within themselves,
for they had not understood about the loaves; rather, their hearts were hardened.
When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored there.
As they got out of the boat, people at once recognized him
and ran about that whole region and began to carry those who were ill around on their mats to wherever they heard he was.
And wherever he went, into villages or towns or farms, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him to let them touch even the fringe of his cloak. And all who touched it were made well.

note.traditional: the border of his garment; the hem of his garment

verse.note: The word can mean simply the edge of a garment. It is also the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their cloaks in obedience to Numbers 15:38–39. Either may be meant here.

verse.text: The Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around him.
They saw that some of his disciples were eating their bread with defiled hands, that is, unwashed.
verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means “common” or “shared.” In Jewish Greek it had come to mean ritually impure, the opposite of holy, and Mark explains it for readers unfamiliar with that usage. The issue is ritual purity, not hygiene; the related verb is rendered “defile” from verse 15 onward.

verse.text: For the Pharisees, and indeed all the Jews, do not eat unless they wash their hands with the fist, holding to the tradition of the elders;
verse.note: The Greek says literally “with the fist,” and what that meant is uncertain. Suggestions include washing with a cupped hand, with a fistful of water, up to the wrist, or by rubbing a fist in the other palm; many versions paraphrase as “thoroughly” or “ceremonially.” Some manuscripts replace the word with one meaning “often,” which suggests that early copyists were also puzzled.

verse.text: and when they come from the marketplace they do not eat unless they immerse themselves. And there are many other things that they have received to hold to: the immersing of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and dining couches.
verse.note: The verb is the one elsewhere rendered “baptize”; its ordinary sense is to dip or immerse, and it is a different word from the one for washing hands in verse 3. Most versions say “wash,” and the standard lexicons allow that sense for ritual purification; the related noun is rendered “immersing” later in the verse. Some early manuscripts read “sprinkle” instead. The clause could also mean that they immerse what they bring from the marketplace, though that is the less common view.

note.traditional: tables (KJV); dining couches; omitted in many modern versions

verse.note: The words “and dining couches” are absent from several important early manuscripts, and many modern versions omit them or move them to a footnote. The SBLGNT includes them. The word can mean a bed or the couch on which diners reclined.

verse.text: So the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat their bread with defiled hands?”
He said to them, “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me;

text.q: in vain do they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines.’
You let go of the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “How well you set aside the commandment of God in order to keep your tradition!

text.q: For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must be put to death.’
But you say that if someone tells his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban,’ that is, a gift,

verse.note: Corban is a Hebrew word for an offering dedicated to God, which Mark translates for his readers as “gift.” Declaring property Corban placed it under a vow, so that the person named—here a parent—could no longer benefit from it. Exactly how such vows worked in practice in this period is debated.

text.q: then you no longer let him do anything for his father or mother,
nullifying the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And you do many things like this.”

verse.text: Then he called the crowd to him again and said to them, “Listen to me, all of you, and understand.

text.q: There is nothing outside a person that by going in can defile that person; rather, the things that come out of a person are what defile the person.”

verse.note: Verse 16 (“If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear”) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not in the SBLGNT text, so the numbering passes from 15 to 17. It was probably added by copyists from similar sayings elsewhere in Mark.

verse.text: When he had left the crowd and gone into a house, his disciples asked him about the parable.
And he said to them, “Are you too so lacking in understanding? Do you not see that nothing that goes into a person from outside can defile that person,
because it goes not into the heart but into the stomach, and then out into the latrine?” Thus he declared all foods clean.

note.term: Thus he declared all foods clean.
note.traditional: purging all meats (KJV); Thus he declared all foods clean (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek is a brief participial phrase, literally “cleansing all foods.” In the earliest manuscripts the participle is masculine, and most scholars connect it with “he said” in verse 18, as Mark’s own comment on what Jesus’s teaching implied. Later manuscripts have a neuter form, which makes the phrase part of Jesus’s words about digestion purging food; the King James Version follows that reading.

verse.text: And he said, “What comes out of a person, that is what defiles the person.

text.q: For from within, out of people’s hearts, come evil designs: acts of sexual immorality, thefts, murders,
adulteries, acts of greed, wicked deeds, deceit, debauchery, a grudging eye, slander, arrogance, folly.

verse.note: Literally “an evil eye,” a Semitic idiom for a stingy or envious disposition (compare Deuteronomy 15:9 and Matthew 20:15). The literal phrase now suggests a curse cast by a look, which is not the point here. Many modern versions simply say “envy.”

text.q: All these wicked things come from within and defile the person.”

verse.text: From there he set out and went away to the region of Tyre. He went into a house and did not want anyone to know it, yet he could not escape notice.
Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him at once, and she came and fell down at his feet.
Now the woman was a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth, and she kept asking him to drive the demon out of her daughter.
verse.note: “Greek” here marks the woman as a Gentile of Greek language and culture, not as someone from Greece. “Syrophoenician” identifies her as a native of the Phoenician coast, which belonged to the Roman province of Syria.

verse.text: He said to her, “Let the children eat their fill first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
verse.note: The Greek word is a diminutive, and some take it to mean small house dogs or puppies, softening the saying. Diminutives in the Greek of this period had often lost their force, and Mark uses several in this passage, so many scholars doubt that any softening is intended. In the image, “the children” are Israel and the dogs are Gentiles.

verse.text: But she answered him, “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.”
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary respectful address to a man, like “sir,” and also the word for “Lord.” From a Gentile stranger the everyday sense is the natural one, though many versions print “Lord” and Mark’s readers may well have heard more in it. In the text followed here, this is the only place in Mark where Jesus is addressed with this word.

verse.text: And he said to her, “Because of that answer, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.”
She went away to her home and found the child lying on the bed and the demon gone.
Leaving the region of Tyre again, he went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the middle of the region of the Decapolis.
verse.note: Sidon lies north of Tyre, while the Sea of Galilee and the Decapolis lie to the southeast, so the route described is a wide loop through largely Gentile territory. The Decapolis (“Ten Cities”) was a group of Hellenistic cities, most of them east of the Jordan.

verse.text: They brought him a man who was deaf and could hardly speak, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.

note.traditional: had an impediment in his speech

verse.note: This rare word occurs only here in the New Testament and once in the Greek version of Isaiah (35:6), in a passage promising that the ears of the deaf will be opened and the tongue of the speechless will sing. Mark’s choice of the word, together with the crowd’s acclamation in verse 37, probably points to that prophecy.

verse.text: Taking him aside, away from the crowd, he put his fingers into the man’s ears, and after spitting he touched the man’s tongue.
Then, looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” which means, “Be opened.”
And his ears were opened, the bond on his tongue was loosed, and he began to speak plainly.
He ordered them to tell no one; but the more he ordered them, all the more they proclaimed it.
They were astounded beyond all measure, saying, “He has done everything well; he makes both the deaf hear and the speechless speak.”
In those days, when there was again a large crowd and they had nothing to eat, he called the disciples to him and said to them,

text.q: “I feel compassion for the crowd, because they have stayed with me three days now and have nothing to eat.
If I send them away hungry to their homes, they will collapse on the way—and some of them have come from far away.”

verse.text: His disciples answered him, “Where could anyone get enough bread to satisfy these people here in a deserted place?”
He asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.”
He directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. Then he took the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people, and they set them before the crowd.
They also had a few small fish; and after blessing them, he said that these too were to be set before them.
They ate and were satisfied, and they picked up the leftover pieces—seven large baskets.
verse.note: The Greek word here names a different kind of basket from the one used in the feeding of the five thousand, generally a larger hamper; the same word is used for the basket in which Paul was lowered from the wall of Damascus. Mark keeps the two words apart again in verses 19 and 20, so the translation distinguishes them as well.

verse.text: There were about four thousand people. And he sent them away.
Immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
verse.note: The place is otherwise unknown. The parallel account in Matthew names “Magadan” instead, and some manuscripts of Mark substitute that name or “Magdala.” It was presumably on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, but its location is uncertain.

verse.text: The Pharisees came out and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven, to test him.
verse.note: Older English versions have “tempting him.” The verb means to put someone to the test, here by a demand meant to discredit him, and most modern translations also use “test” in this verse.

verse.text: Sighing deeply in his spirit, he said, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.”

note.term: no sign will be given to this generation

verse.note: The Greek is literally “if a sign will be given to this generation,” a Hebrew-style oath formula in which the penalty clause is left unspoken. It amounts to an emphatic denial, and translations regularly render it as one.

verse.text: And leaving them, he got into the boat again and went away to the other side.
Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and except for one loaf they had none with them in the boat.
And he warned them, saying, “Watch out! Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.”
verse.note: Leaven was a piece of fermented dough kept back to raise the next batch, and it was a common image for a small influence that works through the whole, often a corrupting one. Many modern versions say “yeast”; “leaven” is kept as the more exact term. Mark does not say what the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod is, though the parallels in Matthew and Luke each give an explanation.

verse.text: And they were discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.
Aware of this, he said to them, “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened?

text.q: Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember,

verse.text: when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of pieces you picked up?” They said to him, “Twelve.”
“And when I broke the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full of pieces did you pick up?” And they said to him, “Seven.”
And he said to them, “Do you not yet understand?”
They came to Bethsaida. And some people brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him.
He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village; and after spitting on his eyes and laying his hands on him, he asked him, “Do you see anything?”
He looked up and said, “I see people; I see them like trees, walking around.”
Then he laid his hands on his eyes again; and the man looked intently, and his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly.
And he sent him home, saying, “Do not even go into the village.”

note.term: “Do not even go into the village.”

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add “nor tell anyone in the village,” and others combine the two commands in different ways. The shorter reading translated here has the earliest support and is the one adopted in most modern editions.

verse.text: Jesus and his disciples went out to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?”
They told him, “John the Baptist; and others say Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets.”
And he asked them, “But you—who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Messiah.”
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “the Christ.” The Greek word translates the Hebrew title for the anointed king Israel expected, and Peter is using it as a title, not a name, which “Messiah” conveys to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it functions as a name.

verse.text: And he sternly ordered them to tell no one about him.
Then he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise.
He said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean speaking without figures or reserve, or speaking in public view. The King James Version has “openly”; most modern translations have “plainly,” which suits the contrast with Jesus’ earlier indirect teaching. On either reading the point is that he held nothing back.

verse.text: But he turned and, seeing his disciples, rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God but on the things of people.”
Then he called the crowd to him along with his disciples and said to them, “If anyone wants to come after me, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.

text.q: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake and for the sake of the good news will save it.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today sounds like a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

text.q: For what does it profit a person to gain the whole world and forfeit their life?

verse.note: Many versions switch to “soul” in verses 36 and 37, while others keep “life.” The Greek word is the same one translated “life” in verse 35, and the argument depends on that continuity. In first-century usage it most often means a person’s life or living self and not an immaterial part of them, though the saying plainly has more in view than physical survival.

text.q: For what could a person give in exchange for their life?

For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of that person when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”

verse.note: In the prophets, Israel’s unfaithfulness to God is regularly pictured as a wife’s adultery. The word carries that sense here: a generation unfaithful to God. It is not a comment on sexual conduct in particular.

verse.text: And he said to them, “Truly I tell you, there are some of those standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see that the kingdom of God has come in power.”
verse.note: Jesus does not say which event he means. Proposals include the transformation on the mountain that follows immediately, the resurrection, the coming of the Spirit, and the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70; others take the saying as expecting the end within a generation. The Greek tense pictures the kingdom as already arrived when it is seen.

verse.text: After six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John with him and led them up a high mountain, privately, by themselves. And he was transformed in front of them,
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for a change of form, the same one usually translated “be transformed” in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18. “Transfigured” comes from the Latin translation and survives in English almost only as a name for this event, which is why most versions keep it. The meaning is not in dispute.

verse.text: and his clothes became dazzling, intensely white, as no launderer on earth could whiten them.
And Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.
Peter spoke up and said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
verse.note: The word is the plain Greek for a tent. The Greek Old Testament uses it both for Israel’s wilderness sanctuary and for the huts of the Feast of Booths, and either echo may be heard here. Older versions have “tabernacles”; modern ones vary among “tents”, “shelters” and “dwellings”.

verse.text: For he did not know what to say, because they had become terrified.
Then a cloud came, overshadowing them, and a voice came from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.”
Suddenly, when they looked around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus alone.
As they were coming down from the mountain, he ordered them not to tell anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.
They kept the matter to themselves, debating what this rising from the dead meant.
And they asked him, “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
He said to them, “Elijah does come first and restores all things. How then is it written about the Son of Man that he must suffer much and be treated with contempt?

text.q: But I tell you that Elijah has in fact come, and they did to him whatever they wanted, just as it is written about him.”

verse.note: The scribes’ teaching rests on Malachi 4:5–6, which promises that Elijah will be sent before the day of the Lord. Jesus’ reply points to John the Baptist, whose execution Mark has already told in chapter 6; Matthew’s parallel says so outright. Which Scripture is meant by “as it is written about him” is uncertain, though many point to the persecution of Elijah by Ahab and Jezebel in 1 Kings 19.

verse.text: When they came to the disciples, they saw a large crowd around them and scribes debating with them.
At once the whole crowd, when they saw him, were utterly amazed, and they ran up and greeted him.
He asked them, “What are you debating with them?”
Someone from the crowd answered him, “Teacher, I brought my son to you. He has a mute spirit,

text.q: and wherever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams at the mouth and grinds his teeth and goes rigid. I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able to.”

verse.text: He answered them, “You unbelieving generation! How long am I to be with you? How long am I to put up with you? Bring him to me.”
They brought the boy to him. When the spirit saw Jesus, it immediately threw the boy into convulsions, and he fell to the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth.
Jesus asked his father, “How long has this been happening to him?” He said, “Since childhood.

text.q: It has often thrown him even into fire and into water to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.”

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “‘If you can’! All things are possible for the one who believes.”
verse.note: Jesus picks up the father’s own words from the previous verse; the Greek marks them as a quotation. Many later manuscripts add “believe”, giving the reading familiar from the King James Version, “If you can believe, all things are possible”. The shorter text has the earliest support and is followed by nearly all modern editions.

verse.text: Immediately the child’s father cried out, “I believe; help my unbelief!”
When Jesus saw that a crowd was rapidly gathering, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you: come out of him and never enter him again.”
After crying out and convulsing him violently, it came out. The boy became like a dead body, so that most of them were saying that he had died.
But Jesus took him by the hand and raised him, and he stood up.
When he had gone into a house, his disciples asked him privately, “Why could we not cast it out?”
He said to them, “This kind can come out by nothing except prayer.”
verse.note: Most manuscripts read “prayer and fasting”, as in the King James Version. The words “and fasting” are missing from a few of the earliest witnesses, and most modern editions judge them an early addition reflecting church practice. The manuscript support for the longer reading is nonetheless broad.

verse.text: They went on from there and were passing through Galilee, and he did not want anyone to know it,
for he was teaching his disciples and telling them, “The Son of Man is being handed over into human hands, and they will kill him, and after he is killed, he will rise after three days.”
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s power, and Mark uses it in turn for what Judas, the chief priests and Pilate each do to Jesus. “Betrayed”, found in some versions, names a treachery the context may supply but the word itself does not state. The Greek also plays on “Son of Man” and “hands of men”, which “human hands” partly preserves.

verse.text: But they did not understand the saying, and they were afraid to ask him.
They came to Capernaum. When he was in the house, he asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?”
But they were silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest.
He sat down, called the Twelve, and said to them, “If anyone wants to be first, that person must be last of all and servant of all.”
Then he took a little child and stood the child in their midst, and taking the child in his arms, he said to them,

text.q: “Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes not me but the one who sent me.”

verse.text: John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.”
But Jesus said, “Do not stop him, for there is no one who will do a deed of power in my name and soon afterward be able to speak evil of me.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary word for power, here used of a single act that displays it. “Miracle” is an accurate rendering and the meaning is not disputed. “Deed of power” is chosen so that the link with “power” elsewhere, as in verse 1, stays visible.

text.q: For whoever is not against us is for us.
For whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ—truly I tell you, that person will certainly not lose their reward.
And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for that person to have a great millstone hung around the neck and to be thrown into the sea.

note.term: causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble

verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament the related noun is used for a snare or obstacle, and the verb means to bring about someone’s fall in loyalty to God. The King James “offend” now suggests hurt feelings, and “cause to sin”, used in some modern versions, is narrower than the Greek. Several current translations also have “cause to stumble”.
Literally “a donkey millstone”: the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey, as distinct from the small hand mill used in a household.

text.q: And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than to have two hands and go away into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire.

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, which the Old Testament associates with child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31–32) and which by Jesus’ time had become a name for the place of final judgment. Most translations render it “hell”, usually with a footnote giving the name. The name is kept here because “hell” merges it with Hades and with later imagery.

text.q: And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than to have two feet and be thrown into Gehenna.
And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into Gehenna,
where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.

note.term: their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched

verse.note: The words echo the last verse of Isaiah (66:24), which pictures the corpses of those who rebelled against God. Many later manuscripts repeat this sentence after verses 43 and 45, where the King James tradition numbers it as verses 44 and 46. The earliest witnesses have it only here, so modern editions omit those two verses and the numbering skips them.

text.q: For everyone will be salted with fire.

note.term: everyone will be salted with fire

verse.note: Many manuscripts add “and every sacrifice will be salted with salt”, drawing on Leviticus 2:13; the short form translated here has the earliest support and is generally preferred. The saying itself is obscure. It is commonly read either of the fire of judgment just mentioned or of a purifying trial that disciples must undergo, and the question remains open.

text.q: Salt is good; but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”

verse.text: He set out from there and went into the region of Judea and across the Jordan. Crowds again gathered around him, and, as was his custom, he again taught them.
They asked him whether it is lawful for a man to divorce his wife, testing him.

note.traditional: Pharisees came up and asked him

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “Pharisees came up and asked him,” as in the parallel at Matthew 19:3, and most English versions follow them. The SBLGNT follows the witnesses that leave the questioners unnamed, judging that “Pharisees” was brought in from Matthew.

The verb means to put someone to the test, here with a question meant to trap. Older versions have “tempting,” which now suggests enticement to sin; most modern translations also use “test” in this verse.

verse.text: He answered them, “What did Moses command you?”
They said, “Moses permitted a man to write a certificate of dismissal and divorce her.”
But Jesus said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote this commandment for you.

text.q: But from the beginning of creation ‘he made them male and female.’
‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife,

note.term: and be united to his wife

verse.note: Some important early manuscripts lack these words, and some critical editions bracket them. They may have been added to complete the quotation of Genesis 2:24, or dropped by a copyist’s slip of the eye. The SBLGNT prints them without brackets.

text.q: and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two but one flesh.
Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

verse.text: In the house the disciples asked him about this again.
He said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her,

text.q: and if she divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery.”

verse.note: In ordinary Jewish practice of the period only a husband could initiate a divorce, whereas Roman law allowed a wife to do so. Only Mark records this half of the saying. Many scholars think it applies Jesus’ teaching to the wider Greco-Roman setting of Mark’s readers, though this is not certain.

verse.text: People were bringing children to him so that he might touch them, but the disciples rebuked them.
When Jesus saw this, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the children come to me; do not stop them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will never enter it.”

verse.note: The Greek can mean “as a child receives it” or “as one receives a child.” Most interpreters and translations take the first sense, which the English word order here also suggests. The second would tie the saying to Jesus’ welcome of the children in this scene.

verse.text: And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
As he was setting out on the road, a man ran up, knelt before him, and asked him, “Good teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.

text.q: You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not give false testimony; do not defraud; honor your father and mother.’”

verse.note: Unlike the rest of the list, this is not one of the Ten Commandments. The verb is used of withholding what is owed to someone, such as wages. It may stand in for the commandment against coveting or echo laws against cheating workers; Matthew and Luke do not include it in their parallels.

verse.text: He said to him, “Teacher, I have kept all these since my youth.”
Jesus looked at him and loved him, and said to him, “One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”
