But his face fell at these words, and he went away grieving, for he had many possessions.
Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How hard it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!”
The disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God!

note.term: how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God
note.traditional: how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God

verse.note: Many manuscripts add “for those who trust in riches,” and the King James Version follows them. The shorter reading, found in some of the earliest witnesses, makes the statement general. Most modern editions and translations adopt it.

text.q: It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: They were utterly astounded and said to one another, “Then who can be saved?”
Jesus looked at them and said, “With people it is impossible, but not with God; for all things are possible with God.”
Peter began to say to him, “Look, we have left everything and followed you.”
Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for my sake and for the sake of the good news
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has since become a religious term and the name of a kind of book, so “good news” is used here. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

text.q: who will not receive a hundred times as much now, in this present time—houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life.

note.term: in the age to come, eternal life

verse.note: “Eternal” translates an adjective formed from the word for “age” in the same sentence. In Jewish usage of the period, eternal life is the life of the coming age, set here against “this present time.” It describes the kind of life as well as its length, and “eternal” remains the standard rendering.

text.q: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

verse.text: They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them; they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Taking the Twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him:

text.q: “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles,

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s custody, and it occurs twice in this verse: Jesus is handed over to the priests, who hand him over to the Gentiles. Older versions have “delivered,” and many use “betrayed” where Judas is in view. One rendering is kept here so that the chain of handings-over stays visible.

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. Here it refers in practice to the Roman authorities. The same word appears in verse 42.

text.q: and they will mock him and spit on him and flog him and kill him, and after three days he will rise.”

verse.text: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.”
He said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said to him, “Grant us to sit, one at your right and one at your left, in your glory.”
But Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?”
verse.note: In Israel’s Scriptures a cup is a common image for the lot God gives someone to undergo, often suffering or judgment. “Baptism” here is likewise a figure: the verb could be used of being plunged into or overwhelmed by calamity. Both images point to Jesus’ coming death.

verse.text: They said to him, “We are able.” Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized you will be baptized,

text.q: but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to grant; it is for those for whom it has been prepared.”

verse.text: When the ten heard this, they began to be indignant with James and John.
Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those who are regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones wield authority over them.

text.q: But it is not so among you. Rather, whoever wants to become great among you will be your servant,
and whoever wants to be first among you will be slave of all.
For even the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

verse.note: The word was used for the price paid to free a slave or a captive, and in the Septuagint for payments that redeem a life or property. The preposition translated “for” commonly means “in place of” or “in exchange for.” How far the image should be pressed, and to whom any payment is made, is debated.

verse.text: They came to Jericho. As he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a sizable crowd, Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting beside the road.
When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out, “Son of David, Jesus, have mercy on me!”
Many rebuked him, telling him to be silent, but he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” So they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take courage! Get up; he is calling you.”
Throwing off his cloak, he jumped up and came to Jesus.
Jesus answered him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabbouni, let me see again.”
verse.note: Mark gives the Aramaic word untranslated, and it is kept here as he has it. It is a heightened form of “Rabbi,” meaning “my master” or “my teacher”; John 20:16 glosses it as “Teacher.” Many English versions substitute “Rabbi” or “My teacher.”

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Go; your faith has saved you.” Immediately he could see again, and he followed him on the road.
verse.note: The verb covers both rescue from illness or danger and salvation in the fuller sense. It is the same word the disciples use in verse 26 (“who can be saved?”). Most versions render “made you well” or “healed you” here; “saved” keeps the link, and many interpreters think Mark intends both senses.

verse.text: When they were approaching Jerusalem, at Bethphage and Bethany near the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
and said to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it.

text.q: And if anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord needs it and will send it back here right away.’”

note.traditional: The Lord has need of it

verse.note: The Greek word means “lord”, “master” or “owner”, and the phrase can also be construed as “its owner needs it”. Most translations take it as a reference to Jesus, as here, though whether bystanders would have heard a title or simply “the master” is uncertain. The promise to send the colt back is taken as part of the message the disciples are to give.

verse.text: They went off and found a colt tied at a door, outside in the street, and they untied it.
Some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?”
They answered just as Jesus had told them, and the people let them go.
They brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks over it, and he sat on it.
Many people spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches they had cut in the fields.
Those who went ahead and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
verse.note: A Hebrew or Aramaic expression meaning “save, please”, taken from Psalm 118:25. The next line, “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord”, is from Psalm 118:26, a psalm sung at the pilgrim festivals. By the first century the word seems to have become a shout of acclamation as well as a plea, and Mark leaves it untranslated.

text.q: Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!”

verse.text: He entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. After looking around at everything, since the hour was already late, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve.
The next day, as they were leaving Bethany, he was hungry.
Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see whether he might find anything on it. But when he came to it he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.

note.term: it was not the season for figs
note.traditional: it was not the season for figs

verse.note: Passover falls in spring, well before the main fig harvest, though a tree in full leaf might carry small early figs. Mark splits the fig tree story around the temple incident, and most interpreters read the two together, with the fruitless tree as an acted sign about the temple. How far Mark intends that symbolism is debated.

verse.text: In response he said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples were listening.

They came to Jerusalem. Entering the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling and those who were buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves,
verse.note: The word covers the whole temple complex, not just the sanctuary building. The trading took place in the large outer court, the only area open to non-Jews. Money changers exchanged everyday coinage for the currency accepted for temple dues, and doves were sold as sacrificial offerings, especially for the poor.

verse.text: and he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.
He was teaching them and saying, “Is it not written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of bandits.”
verse.note: The quotation is from Isaiah 56:7. The Greek word for “nations” is the same one this translation elsewhere renders “Gentiles”. In the plural it means the non-Jewish peoples, which gives the saying its point in the court to which they were admitted.

note.traditional: a den of robbers (KJV: a den of thieves)

verse.note: The phrase echoes Jeremiah 7:11. The Greek word denotes a violent, often armed plunderer such as a highwayman or brigand, not a sneak thief or a cheating trader, and the “den” is the cave where such men hide out. Most modern translations have “robbers”; “bandits” is used here to keep the note of violence and outlawry and to match the same word at the arrest and crucifixion.

verse.text: The chief priests and the scribes heard this and began looking for a way to destroy him; for they were afraid of him, because the whole crowd was astonished at his teaching.
When evening came, they went out of the city.
verse.note: The Greek conjunction usually means “whenever”, and the verb is in a tense that can describe repeated action, so the sentence may mean “Whenever evening came, they would go out of the city”, describing the routine of the whole week. In the Greek of this period the same construction can also refer to a single occasion, which is how it is taken here. Translations and commentators are divided.

verse.text: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots up.
Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree you cursed has withered.”
Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “have faith of God”. Nearly all interpreters take God as the object of the faith, as here. A few have read it as “hold on to God’s faithfulness”, but the following verses about believing and not doubting favor the usual reading.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in their heart but believes that what they say will happen, it will be done for them.
For this reason I tell you, whatever you pray and ask for, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
And whenever you stand praying, if you have anything against anyone, forgive it, so that your Father in the heavens may also forgive you your offenses.”

verse.note: The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have recognized. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it.

The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespasses” is the rendering of the Tyndale and King James tradition and of several modern versions, but in current English it mainly suggests entering property without permission. The meaning is not disputed, only the best English word, and “offense” is a standard lexicon gloss.

Many later manuscripts add a verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in the heavens forgive your offenses.” It is absent from the earliest and best witnesses and is generally thought to have been added under the influence of Matthew 6:15. The Greek text translated here omits it, which is why the numbering passes from 25 to 27.

verse.text: They came again to Jerusalem. As he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes and the elders came to him
and said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things? Or who gave you this authority to do them?”
Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question. Answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.

text.q: John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from people? Answer me.”

verse.note: “Heaven” here is a reverent Jewish way of saying “God”. The question is whether John’s baptism was authorized by God or was a merely human undertaking. The answer bears directly on Jesus’ own authority, since John had pointed to him.

verse.text: They argued it out among themselves, saying, “What should we say? If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’
But should we say, ‘From people’?” They were afraid of the crowd, for everyone held that John really was a prophet.
So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”
And he began to speak to them in parables: “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a vat for the winepress, and built a watchtower. Then he leased it to tenants and went abroad.
verse.note: The fence, vat, and tower echo the song of the vineyard in Isaiah 5, where the vineyard is Israel and its owner is God. A hearer who knew the Scriptures would have recognized the allusion at once and understood the tenants as those entrusted with God’s people.

text.q: When the season came, he sent a slave to the tenants to collect from them some of the fruit of the vineyard.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and first-century readers would have understood it so. Many traditional versions use “servant,” which softens the social reality; a number of modern translations now use “slave.”

text.q: But they took him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.
Again he sent another slave to them; that one they struck on the head and treated shamefully.

verse.note: This verb is extremely rare and its exact meaning is uncertain. It is evidently formed from the word for “head,” and most translators take it as “struck on the head” or “wounded in the head”; a few have suggested “dealt with summarily.”

text.q: He sent another, and that one they killed; and so with many others, beating some and killing others.
He still had one, a beloved son. He sent him to them last, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’
So they took him and killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.
What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.
Have you not even read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone;

verse.note: The Greek is literally “head of the corner,” quoting Psalm 118:22. It may mean a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the capstone that completes an arch or wall. Scholars are divided; either way it is the stone on which the structure depends.

text.q: this came from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”

verse.text: And they were looking for a way to arrest him, but they feared the crowd, for they knew that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
Then they sent some of the Pharisees and the Herodians to him, to trap him in something he said.
verse.note: The Herodians were evidently supporters of the Herodian dynasty, which ruled by Roman favor; little else is known of them. Their pairing with the Pharisees sharpens the trap: a “no” to the tax could be reported as sedition, while a “yes” would discredit Jesus with the people.

verse.text: They came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and are swayed by no one, for you pay no regard to people’s standing but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay the tax to Caesar or not? Should we pay, or should we not pay?”
verse.note: The Greek word is borrowed from the Latin census and refers to the head tax Rome levied on Judea after it came under direct Roman rule. The tax was deeply resented and had provoked armed revolt when it was introduced. The denarius Jesus asks for was a Roman silver coin bearing the emperor’s portrait and titles.

verse.text: But he, knowing their hypocrisy, said to them, “Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius so that I can look at it.”
verse.note: The older English tradition has “Why tempt ye me?” The Greek verb means to put to the test, here with the aim of trapping, and “tempt” now suggests enticement to sin. Most modern translations also use “test” in this verse.

verse.text: They brought one. And he said to them, “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.”
Then Jesus said to them, “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” And they were utterly amazed at him.
verse.note: The questioners asked whether to “give” the tax; Jesus answers with a compound verb meaning to give back or pay what is owed. Traditional versions have “render,” which is accurate but now obscure, and many modern ones simply have “give.” The implication is that the coin, bearing Caesar’s image, already belongs to him.

verse.text: Then some Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to him and put a question to him:

text.q: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife behind but leaves no child, the man is to take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.
There were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and when he died he left no offspring.
The second took her and died, leaving no offspring behind, and the third likewise.
None of the seven left offspring. Last of all, the woman died too.
In the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.”

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Is this not why you are mistaken: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God?

text.q: For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in the heavens.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase for God’s dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; the plural is kept here because the Greek has it.

text.q: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?

note.term: in the passage about the bush

verse.note: The Greek says simply “at the bush.” Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage was cited by its subject; this is the account of the burning bush in Exodus 3. Jesus argues from the Law of Moses, which the Sadducees acknowledged as authoritative.

text.q: He is not God of the dead but of the living. You are badly mistaken.”

verse.text: One of the scribes came up and heard them debating. Seeing that Jesus had answered them well, he asked him, “Which commandment is first of all?”
verse.note: The traditional word “scribes” is kept, but these were not copyists. They were trained scholars and teachers of the Law of Moses, recognized as authorities on its interpretation.

verse.text: Jesus answered, “The first is, ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one;

note.term: the Lord our God, the Lord is one
note.traditional: The Lord our God is one Lord

verse.note: This is the opening of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), recited daily by observant Jews. The Greek, like the Hebrew behind it, can be construed in several ways: “the Lord our God is one Lord,” “the Lord our God, the Lord is one,” or “the Lord is our God, the Lord alone.” The scribe’s reply in verse 32 (“he is one”) favors the rendering chosen here.

text.q: and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’
The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”

verse.text: And the scribe said to him, “Well said, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him;

text.q: and to love him with all one’s heart and with all one’s understanding and with all one’s strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is far more than all the whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.”

verse.text: When Jesus saw that he had answered thoughtfully, he said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to question him any longer.
As Jesus was teaching in the temple, he responded by saying, “How can the scribes say that the Messiah is the son of David?
verse.note: The Greek word, traditionally “Christ,” is here a title under discussion: the anointed king Israel expected. “Messiah” conveys the title to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

text.q: David himself said by the Holy Spirit, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet.”’

verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 110:1. Many manuscripts read “a footstool for your feet,” matching the Greek Old Testament; the text translated here reads “under your feet,” which is probably the earlier wording in Mark, later conformed to the psalm.

verse.text: David himself calls him ‘Lord’; so how can he be his son?” And the large crowd was listening to him with delight.
And in his teaching he said, “Beware of the scribes, who want to walk around in long robes, and want greetings in the marketplaces

text.q: and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.
They devour widows’ houses and for show make long prayers. These will receive a more severe judgment.”

verse.text: He sat down opposite the treasury and watched how the crowd was putting money into the treasury. Many rich people were putting in large sums.
Then one poor widow came and put in two tiny coins, which make a quadrans.
verse.note: The widow’s coins were lepta, the smallest coins in circulation. Mark explains their value for his readers in Roman terms: together they equaled a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, one sixty-fourth of a denarius, which was roughly a laborer’s daily wage.

verse.text: Calling his disciples to him, he said to them, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are putting into the treasury.

text.q: For they all put in out of their surplus, but she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had—her whole livelihood.”

verse.text: As he was going out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Teacher, look—what stones and what buildings!”
And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down.”
As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked him privately,

text.q: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?”

verse.text: Jesus began to say to them, “Watch out that no one leads you astray.

text.q: Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and they will lead many astray.

verse.note: The Greek is simply “I am,” with no complement. In context it most naturally means “I am the one,” that is, the Messiah, which is how Matthew’s parallel spells it out. Some scholars also hear an echo of the divine self-declaration “I am” from the Greek Old Testament; the wording allows this, but it cannot be proved.

text.q: When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. It must happen, but the end is not yet.
For nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom; there will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These things are the beginning of the birth pains.

verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is often translated “Gentiles,” the non-Jewish peoples. In this verse and in “all the nations” in verse 10 it means peoples as such, so “nation” is used. The reader should know that one Greek word lies behind both English words across the New Testament.

The word means the pains of a woman in labor. The prophets used labor as an image for the anguish that comes before God’s deliverance, and later Jewish writers spoke in similar terms of the suffering that would precede the age to come. The image implies that the pain leads to something and is not the end itself.

text.q: But you, watch out for yourselves. They will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them.

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s custody. Mark uses the same word for what Judas, the chief priests, and Pilate do to Jesus, so one rendering is kept throughout to let the reader see that the disciples’ fate mirrors their teacher’s. Many versions vary it with “deliver up,” “arrest,” or “betray” (as in verse 12).

text.q: And the good news must first be proclaimed to all the nations.

verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book, so the plainer rendering is used. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

text.q: And when they lead you away to hand you over, do not worry beforehand about what you will say, but say whatever is given to you in that hour, for it is not you who are speaking but the Holy Spirit.
Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and have them put to death.
You will be hated by everyone because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

verse.text: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he should not be (let the reader understand), then those in Judea must flee to the mountains,
verse.note: The phrase comes from the book of Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), where it refers to a detestable object set up in the temple that leaves it defiled and deserted; Jewish readers connected it with the pagan altar erected by Antiochus IV in 167 BC. “Abomination” in the Greek Old Testament regularly means something idolatrous. What event Jesus’ saying points to is disputed: proposals include events of the Jewish war of AD 66–70 and a still-future figure.

note.term: standing where he should not be

verse.note: The noun “abomination” is neuter in Greek, but the participle “standing” is masculine, which suggests that Mark thinks of a person. Most English versions smooth this over with “it”; the masculine is kept here because the grammatical mismatch appears deliberate. It is possible, though less likely, that the masculine is merely loose grammar.

This is usually taken as an aside by Mark to the person reading the Gospel aloud to a congregation, signaling that the cryptic phrase needs careful interpretation; it is labeled as the narrator’s words on that view. It could instead be part of Jesus’ speech, referring to the reader of Daniel. The Greek does not settle the question.

text.q: the one on the housetop must not come down or go inside to take anything out of his house,
and the one in the field must not turn back to get his cloak.
Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days!
Pray that it may not happen in winter.
For those days will be an affliction such as has not happened from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will happen.

verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for oppressive hardship, not a technical name. “Tribulation” is now widely heard as the title of a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. “Affliction” is itself a long-standing rendering of the word and is used for it throughout this translation. The sentence echoes Daniel 12:1.

text.q: And if the Lord had not cut the days short, no flesh would be saved. But for the sake of the chosen ones, whom he chose, he has cut the days short.

verse.note: “All flesh” is a Hebrew idiom for all living people. “Saved” here refers in the first instance to physical survival: no one would come through alive. Many modern versions paraphrase as “no one would survive.”

note.term: the chosen ones, whom he chose

verse.note: The noun and the verb share a root in Greek, and the repetition is deliberate. “The elect” hides that link and has become a term of later theological debate; “chosen ones” is what the word plainly means and echoes the Old Testament’s language for Israel as God’s chosen people. Many versions keep “the elect.”

text.q: And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Messiah!’ or ‘Look, there!’ do not believe it.

verse.note: The Greek word, traditionally rendered “Christ,” translates the Hebrew “Messiah,” the anointed king Israel expected. Here it is a title under discussion, not a name, so “Messiah” is used; “false messiahs” in verse 22 is a compound of the same word. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

text.q: For false messiahs and false prophets will arise and will give signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the chosen ones.
But you, watch out. I have told you everything beforehand.
But in those days, after that affliction, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light,
and the stars will be falling from the sky, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.

note.traditional: the powers that are in heaven

verse.note: Verses 24–25 draw on prophetic imagery, especially Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4, where the darkening of sun, moon, and stars accompanies God’s judgment on nations. “The powers in the heavens” are the heavenly bodies, perhaps thought of as the spiritual forces associated with them. Interpreters differ on whether the language describes a literal cosmic collapse or is the prophets’ customary way of depicting world-shaking historical events. The Greek plural “heavens” is kept.

text.q: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.

note.term: the Son of Man coming in clouds
note.traditional: the Son of man coming in the clouds

verse.note: The wording comes from Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion. Most interpreters take the saying here to refer to Jesus’ return; a minority read it, with Daniel, as a coming to God for vindication and enthronement.

text.q: And then he will send out the angels and gather the chosen ones from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.
Learn the parable from the fig tree: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near.
So also you, when you see these things happening, know that he is near, right at the door.

verse.note: The Greek verb has no expressed subject and can mean “he is near” (the Son of Man) or “it is near” (the end, or the event just described). “He” is chosen because of the image of someone at the door and the returning master in verses 34–36. Translations are divided.

text.q: Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.

verse.note: In ordinary usage the word means the people alive at one time, and elsewhere in Mark “this generation” refers to Jesus’ contemporaries. How this fits with what follows is one of the most debated questions in the chapter: some take “all these things” to be the events leading up to the temple’s destruction in AD 70, others take the saying to cover the end itself. Proposals that the word means “race” or “kind of people” have little support in usage of the period.

text.q: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
But about that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but only the Father.
Watch out, stay alert, for you do not know when the time is.

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “stay alert and pray,” and older English versions follow them. The words “and pray” are absent from a few important early witnesses and may have been added under the influence of Mark 14:38. The edition translated here omits them.

text.q: It is like a man away on a journey, who has left his house and given his slaves authority, to each his work, and has commanded the doorkeeper to stay awake.

verse.note: The Greek word means a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. “Servants” softens the picture; the parable assumes a household in which the absent owner’s slaves run his affairs and answer to him on his return. A number of recent translations also use “slaves.”

text.q: So stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house is coming, whether in the evening or at midnight or at cockcrow or at dawn—

note.term: in the evening or at midnight or at cockcrow or at dawn
note.traditional: at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning

verse.note: These are the popular names of the four watches into which the Roman reckoning divided the night, each about three hours long, from sunset to sunrise. The master may return in any of them.

text.q: so that he does not come suddenly and find you sleeping.
And what I say to you I say to everyone: Stay awake.”

verse.text: It was two days before the Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to seize him by deceit and kill him,
for they were saying, “Not during the festival, or there may be an uproar among the people.”

While he was in Bethany, reclining at table in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came with an alabaster flask of perfumed oil—pure nard, very costly. She broke the flask and poured it over his head.
verse.note: The Greek word covers the range of ritually defiling scaly skin conditions regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which is broader than modern leprosy (Hansen’s disease) and may not include it. Elsewhere this translation says “skin disease”; here the traditional word is kept because it works as a byname identifying which Simon is meant. Since he is hosting a dinner, he was presumably no longer afflicted, though the text does not say.

The adjective describing the nard is rare and its meaning is uncertain. Most take it as “genuine” or “pure,” that is, unadulterated; others have suggested it names a variety of the plant or its source. Nard was an aromatic oil imported from the East, which explains its price.

verse.text: But some who were there said indignantly to one another, “Why has this perfumed oil been wasted?
This perfumed oil could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor.” And they scolded her harshly.

note.traditional: three hundred pence; three hundred denarii

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a laborer. Three hundred denarii was therefore close to a year’s wages.

verse.text: But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why are you making trouble for her? She has done a good thing for me.

text.q: For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want you can do good to them, but you do not always have me.
She did what she could: she has anointed my body ahead of time for burial.
Truly I tell you, wherever the good news is proclaimed throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for the public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so the plain meaning is given. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went off to the chief priests to hand him over to them.
verse.note: Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use the same word for what the priests do to Jesus before Pilate and what Pilate then does. “Betray” names the treachery the context supplies, and some scholars defend it as a legitimate contextual sense; “hand over” lets the reader see the repeated word, as in verses 11, 18, 21, 41, 42 and 44.

verse.text: When they heard it they were glad, and they promised to give him money. So he began looking for a good opportunity to hand him over.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed, his disciples said to him, “Where do you want us to go and make preparations for you to eat the Passover?”
He sent two of his disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,

text.q: and wherever he goes in, say to the owner of the house, ‘The Teacher says: Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’
He will show you a large upstairs room, furnished and ready. Make preparations for us there.”

verse.text: The disciples set out and went into the city and found things just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve.
While they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over—one who is eating with me.”
They began to be distressed and to say to him one after another, “Surely not I?”
He said to them, “It is one of the Twelve, the one who dips into the bowl with me.

text.q: For the Son of Man goes as it is written about him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”

verse.text: While they were eating, he took bread, said the blessing, broke it, and gave it to them, and said, “Take it; this is my body.”
Then he took a cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, and they all drank from it.
He said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

text.q: Truly I tell you, I will never again drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: After singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’
verse.note: The older rendering “be offended” now suggests hurt feelings. The verb pictures being tripped up so as to fall from loyalty, and here it refers to the disciples’ desertion that night; most modern versions also say “fall away.” The quotation that follows is from Zechariah 13:7.

text.q: But after I have been raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

verse.text: But Peter said to him, “Even if all fall away, I will not.”
Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today, this very night, before a rooster crows twice, you yourself will deny me three times.”
But he kept saying all the more forcefully, “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you.” And they all said the same.
They came to a place named Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”
He took Peter, James, and John with him, and he began to be gripped by dread and anguish,
and he said to them, “My soul is overwhelmed with grief, to the point of death. Stay here and keep awake.”
Going on a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass him by.
He said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Take this cup away from me. Yet not what I want, but what you want.”
verse.note: Abba is the Aramaic word for “father,” used in addressing one’s own father by children and adults alike. Mark preserves the Aramaic and adds the Greek equivalent. The once-popular claim that it is baby talk equivalent to “Daddy” is no longer widely held.

verse.text: He came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Did you not have the strength to keep awake for one hour?

text.q: Keep awake and pray, so that you do not come into testing. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

verse.note: Most versions have “temptation” here; some have “the time of trial.” In the usage of the period the word chiefly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will remain faithful, which is what the disciples are about to face. English “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin. Lexicons recognize both senses, and the two overlap here.

verse.text: Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.
Again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down, and they did not know what to answer him.
He came the third time and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.

note.term: Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough!
note.traditional: Sleep on now, and take your rest: it is enough

verse.note: The first sentence can be read as a question, as a command (“Sleep on now and rest”), or as a reproachful exclamation. The single Greek word rendered “Enough!” is among the most debated in Mark: its usual meanings were “he has received in full” or “it is distant,” and proposals include “It is settled” and “He has been paid,” referring to Judas. “Enough” is the most common rendering but is uncertain.

text.q: Get up, let us go. Look, the one handing me over has come near.”

verse.text: At once, while he was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders.
Now the one handing him over had given them a signal, saying, “The one I kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard.”
As soon as he arrived, he went up to him and said, “Rabbi!” and kissed him.
Then they laid hands on him and seized him.
But one of those standing by drew his sword, struck the high priest’s slave, and cut off his ear.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. Some modern versions also say “slave.” The same applies to the “slave girls” of verses 66 and 69, where the Greek word means a female slave and is traditionally rendered “maid” or “servant girl.”

verse.text: Jesus responded and said to them, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me, as if against a bandit?
verse.note: The Greek word denotes an armed, violent plunderer such as a highwayman, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and some versions render it “rebel” here; that reading is possible but not certain. Most modern versions have “robber.”

text.q: Day after day I was with you in the temple, teaching, and you did not seize me. But this is so that the Scriptures may be fulfilled.”

verse.text: Then they all left him and fled.
A certain young man was following him, wearing nothing but a linen cloth. They seized him,
but he left the linen cloth behind and fled naked.
They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, the elders, and the scribes came together.
Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the high priest’s courtyard, and he was sitting with the attendants and warming himself at the fire.
Now the chief priests and the whole council were looking for testimony against Jesus in order to put him to death, but they were finding none.
For many were giving false testimony against him, and their testimonies did not agree.
Then some stood up and gave false testimony against him, saying,

text.q: “We heard him say, ‘I will tear down this sanctuary made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.’”

verse.note: Greek has two words usually both rendered “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts (as in verse 49) and this one for the building in which God was held to dwell. “Sanctuary” keeps them distinct. Most versions use “temple” for both, and scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers observe the distinction.

verse.text: Yet even on this point their testimony did not agree.
Then the high priest stood up in their midst and questioned Jesus: “Have you no answer at all? What is it that these men are testifying against you?”
But he stayed silent and gave no answer at all. Again the high priest questioned him and said to him, “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?”
verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one,” the king Israel expected. Here it is a title under examination, not a name, so “Messiah” is used; several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. “Christ” is kept where the word functions as part of Jesus’ name.

verse.text: Jesus said, “I am; and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”
verse.note: “The Power,” like “the Blessed One” in the high priest’s question, is a reverent way of referring to God without naming him. Jesus’ reply combines Psalm 110:1, where the king sits at God’s right hand, with Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven.

verse.text: The high priest tore his clothes and said, “What further need do we have of witnesses?
You have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?” And they all condemned him as deserving death.
Some began to spit on him, to cover his face and strike him with their fists, and to say to him, “Prophesy!” And the attendants received him with slaps.
While Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s slave girls came,
and when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked straight at him and said, “You too were with the Nazarene, Jesus.”
But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you are talking about.” He went outside into the forecourt, and a rooster crowed.
verse.note: These words are missing from several important early manuscripts, and some critical editions bracket them. They may have been added to prepare for the “second time” of verse 72, or removed to match the other Gospels, which mention only one crowing. The Greek text followed here includes them.

verse.text: The slave girl saw him and began again to say to those standing by, “This man is one of them.”
But again he denied it. A little later those standing by again said to Peter, “You really are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech is like theirs.”

note.term: and your speech is like theirs

verse.note: These words are absent from the earliest manuscripts and from most modern translations, though they stand in the majority of later manuscripts and in the King James Version. Many scholars think they were added under the influence of Matthew 26:73. The Greek text followed here includes them.

verse.text: But he began to call down curses and to swear an oath: “I do not know this man you are talking about.”
verse.note: The verb means to place someone under a curse, and no object is expressed. Most understand that Peter invoked a curse on himself if he was lying; some scholars think he cursed Jesus. The traditional “curse and swear” can wrongly suggest profanity, whereas the Greek describes a solemn curse and a sworn denial.

verse.text: At once a rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered what Jesus had said to him: “Before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he broke down and wept.

note.traditional: when he thought thereon, he wept

verse.note: The Greek participle before “wept” is obscure. Proposals include “he broke down,” “he began to,” “when he thought about it,” “he rushed outside,” and “covering his head.” None has won general agreement.

verse.text: And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests, after holding a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council, bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate.
verse.note: The same Greek verb is used for what Judas does to Jesus, what the chief priests do here, and what Pilate does in verse 15. Older versions vary it as “betray” and “deliver”; this translation keeps one rendering so the chain of handings-over stays visible. The standard lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense.

verse.text: Pilate asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” He answered him, “You say so.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally “You say,” with an emphatic “you.” It can be heard as a guarded yes (“It is as you say”) or as a noncommittal reply that leaves the claim in Pilate’s mouth. Most interpreters take it as neither a denial nor a plain affirmation, and the rendering keeps that reserve.

verse.text: And the chief priests were accusing him of many things.
Pilate questioned him again: “Have you no answer at all? See how many charges they are bringing against you.”
But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
Now at each festival he used to release for them one prisoner, the one they asked for.
There was a man called Barabbas, in chains with the rebels who had committed murder in the rebellion.
The crowd came up and began to ask him to do what he usually did for them.
Pilate answered them, “Do you want me to release for you the king of the Jews?”
For he knew that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed him over.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas for them instead.
Pilate spoke to them again: “Then what do you want me to do with the one you call the king of the Jews?”
They shouted back, “Crucify him!”
Pilate said to them, “Why? What wrong has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him!”
So Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas for them; and after having Jesus flogged, he handed him over to be crucified.
The soldiers led him away inside the palace, that is, the praetorium, and called together the whole cohort.

note.term: the palace, that is, the praetorium

verse.note: “Praetorium” is the Latin term for a Roman governor’s official residence and headquarters, and Mark uses it to explain a Greek word that can mean either a courtyard or a palace. Which building in Jerusalem is meant is disputed; Herod’s palace and the Antonia fortress are the usual candidates. A cohort was nominally about six hundred soldiers, though the word may be used loosely here.

verse.text: They dressed him in purple, and they wove a crown of thorns and set it on him.
And they began to salute him: “Hail, king of the Jews!”
They kept striking his head with a reed and spitting on him, and going down on their knees they paid him homage.
verse.note: The Greek verb names prostration in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it. Here soldiers parody the homage owed to a king, and the kneeling is stated separately, so “paid him homage” says what the word says without the religious claim that modern “worship” carries. Many modern versions render similarly here.

verse.text: When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple and put his own clothes on him. Then they led him out to crucify him.
They pressed into service a passerby, a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross.
They brought him to the place Golgotha, which translated means Place of the Skull.
They tried to give him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it.
And they crucified him and divided his clothes among themselves, casting lots for them to decide who would take what.
It was the third hour when they crucified him.
verse.note: Daytime hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning. The sixth hour (verse 33) is about noon, and the ninth hour (verses 33–34) about three in the afternoon.

verse.text: The inscription stating the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews.”
And with him they crucified two bandits, one on his right and one on his left.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes someone who plunders with violence, such as a brigand or highwayman, and is distinct from the word for a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and some versions render it “rebels” here; that reading is possible but not certain. “Bandit” keeps the violence and outlawry without deciding the question.

note.term: one on his right and one on his left

verse.note: Verse 28 (“And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was counted among the lawless’”) is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek text translated here. It is generally regarded as a later addition drawn from Luke 22:37, so the numbering passes from 27 to 29.

verse.text: Those passing by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads and saying, “Ha! You who would destroy the sanctuary and build it in three days,
verse.note: The Greek verb is the source of English “blaspheme,” but in the first century it meant abusive or demeaning speech against anyone, not only against God. Here the abuse is jeering thrown at a man to his face, so “hurled insults at” is used. Modern versions vary among “derided,” “reviled,” and “hurled insults.”

Greek has one word for the whole temple complex with its courts and another, used here and in verse 38, for the sanctuary building itself. Most English versions render both as “temple.” This translation uses “sanctuary” so that the taunt about destroying the sanctuary and the tearing of the sanctuary’s curtain are visibly linked, as they are in Greek.

text.q: save yourself by coming down from the cross!”

verse.text: In the same way the chief priests also, along with the scribes, mocked him among themselves, saying, “He saved others; himself he cannot save!
Let the Messiah, the king of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe.” Those who were crucified with him also taunted him.
verse.note: The Greek word means the anointed king Israel expected, and here it is plainly a title, set beside “the king of Israel.” “Messiah” conveys that title to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

verse.text: When the sixth hour came, darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour.
verse.note: The Greek noun can mean a particular land or region, or the whole earth. Either sense is possible here, and translations are divided; “land” is chosen as the more restrained reading.

verse.text: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which translated means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
verse.note: Jesus’s words are the opening line of Psalm 22, given by Mark in Aramaic and then translated. The same psalm speaks of onlookers who shake their heads in mockery and of clothing divided by lot, both echoed earlier in this chapter. The bystanders’ remark in the next verse turns on the similarity in sound between “Eloi” and the name Elijah.

verse.text: Some of the bystanders heard it and said, “Look, he is calling Elijah!”
Someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, and offered it to him to drink, saying, “Wait! Let us see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”
But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed his last.
And the curtain of the sanctuary was torn in two, from top to bottom.
When the centurion who was standing facing him saw that he had breathed his last in this way, he said, “Truly this man was God’s Son!”
verse.note: The Greek has no article and can be read as “the Son of God” or “a son of God”; a Roman soldier might have meant something like “a son of a god.” Greek grammar often omits the article in this construction even when the sense is definite, and Mark’s readers would hear the title his Gospel has given Jesus from the start. “God’s Son” leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: There were also women watching from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.
When he was in Galilee they used to follow him and serve him; and there were many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem.
When evening had already come, since it was Preparation day, that is, the day before the Sabbath,
Joseph of Arimathea came, a respected member of the council, who was himself also waiting for the kingdom of God. He gathered his courage, went in to Pilate, and asked for the body of Jesus.
Pilate was amazed that he had already died, and summoning the centurion he asked him whether he had been dead for some time.
When he learned it from the centurion, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of rock; then he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where he was laid.
When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they could go and anoint him.
verse.note: The Sabbath ended at sunset on Saturday, so the women could buy spices that evening and set out at first light on Sunday. Anointing a body with aromatic oils was a last act of honor to the dead, not embalming.

verse.text: And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen.
They were saying to one another, “Who will roll the stone away from the entrance of the tomb for us?”
And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away—for it was very large.
Entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verse.note: Mark calls the figure simply a young man. Jewish writings of the period often describe angels as young men in bright or white clothing, and Matthew's parallel account calls the figure an angel. Most interpreters therefore take Mark to mean a heavenly messenger, and his words are marked as an angel's here.

verse.text: But he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. Look—the place where they laid him.

note.traditional: He is risen / He has risen

verse.note: The Greek verb is passive in form. It can be read as a true passive, “he has been raised” (that is, by God), or as an intransitive, “he has risen.” Both are grammatically sound and translations divide; the passive is chosen here because the New Testament regularly speaks of God raising Jesus.

text.q: But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you.’”

verse.note: This refers back to Jesus' words on the way to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:28): “After I am raised, I will go ahead of you to Galilee.”

verse.text: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them. And they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. ⟦But they reported briefly to those around Peter everything they had been commanded. And after this, Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation. Amen.⟧
verse.note: The double brackets mark text that is almost certainly not part of Mark's original Gospel. The two oldest complete manuscripts end at “for they were afraid.” The bracketed sentences here, known as the Shorter Ending, appear in only a handful of manuscripts, usually followed by verses 9–20, and their vocabulary is unlike Mark's. Scholars debate whether Mark meant to end at verse 8 or whether an original ending was lost.

verse.text: ⟦Now when he had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.

note.term: Now when he had risen early

verse.note: Verses 9–20, the Longer Ending, are double-bracketed because the two oldest complete manuscripts lack them, and some early Christian writers reported that many Greek copies known to them did too. The passage is found in the great majority of later manuscripts and was known by the late second century. Its style differs from the rest of Mark, and it seems to summarize appearances told in the other Gospels and Acts. Most scholars consider it an early addition rather than Mark's own work.

verse.text: She went and reported it to those who had been with him, as they were mourning and weeping.
And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe it.
After this he appeared in a different form to two of them as they were walking, on their way into the country.
They too went back and reported it to the rest, but they did not believe them either.

Later he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had been raised.
And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today sounds like a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

text.q: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new languages;

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “new tongues.” The Greek word means the tongue as an organ and, by extension, a language; “tongues” in this sense is now archaic in English outside church usage. “Languages” gives what a first-century reader would have heard, though the nature of the speech meant is debated. Some manuscripts lack the word “new.”

text.q: they will pick up snakes, and if they drink anything deadly it will certainly not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will get well.”

verse.text: So then the Lord Jesus, after speaking to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.
And they went out and proclaimed everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.⟧
